```html
      <h2 class="text-title-sm">Profile</h2>
      <p>Your name appears on invoices and shared projects.</p>
      <button class="btn primary" type="button">Save changes</button>
    </section>
  </div>
</main>
```

Each class does one job:

- `.section` pads the page: a responsive gutter at the sides (1 to 2rem) and generous space above and below (4 to 7rem).
- `.section-content` centers a column with a maximum width; `.narrow` makes that 48rem instead of 80rem, a comfortable width for a form.
- `.stack` lays its children out vertically with a 1rem gap.
- `.text-title` and `.text-title-sm` set heading sizes: 1.875rem bold and 1.25rem semibold.
- `.card` is a bordered container with rounded corners and 1.25rem of padding.
- `.btn` makes a button, and `.primary` gives it the primary color.

Headings are not sized by their tag: the reset gives an `<h1>` with no type class the same size and weight as the text around it. That keeps the document structure, which heading level an element is, separate from the size you want it to look. If you want headings styled automatically, see [Setup → Classless HTML](docs/setup.md#classless-html).

## Lay out the page

Three layout helpers cover most screens, and all three use the same gap, `--layout-gap` (1rem):

- `.stack` for vertical lists of blocks.
- `.cluster` for a row that wraps when it runs out of room, such as a group of buttons. Add `.between` to push the first and last items to opposite ends.
- `.auto-grid` for a grid of equal cards that adds or drops columns as the space changes. A column is never narrower than `--layout-grid-min` (16rem) unless the container itself is.

`.tight` (0.5rem) and `.loose` (1.5rem) change the gap of the layout they sit on. A layout nested inside keeps its own gap.

Add a header and put the buttons in a row:

```html
<main class="section">
  <div class="section-content narrow stack loose">
    <header class="stack tight">
      <h1 class="text-title">Account settings</h1>
      <p>Manage your profile, plan, and security.</p>
    </header>

    <section class="card stack" aria-labelledby="profile-title">
      <h2 class="text-title-sm" id="profile-title">Profile</h2>
      <p>Your name appears on invoices and shared projects.</p>
      <div class="cluster">
        <button class="btn primary" type="button">Save changes</button>
        <button class="btn ghost" type="button">Cancel</button>
      </div>
    </section>
  </div>
</main>
```

[Content and layout](docs/usage/content-and-layout.md) lists every layout helper, including `.view`, `.divider`, and `.visually-hidden`, and the full type scale.

## Intent: which color

The Save button is `.primary` and the Cancel button has no intent, which makes it neutral. An intent class picks a color role:

| Class          | Use it for                            | Default color                           |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| _none_         | Anything without a meaning of its own | The page's text and border grays        |
| `.primary`     | The main action on a screen           | Near-black on light, near-white on dark |
| `.secondary`   | A second, quieter action              | Mid gray                                |
| `.success`     | Confirmation and completed states     | Emerald green                           |
| `.warning`     | Something that needs attention soon   | Amber, with dark text                   |
| `.destructive` | Deleting, revoking, and errors        | Rose red                                |
| `.info`        | Neutral notices and help              | Indigo                                  |

Intent stays on the element that carries it. Putting `.destructive` on a `<section>` does not turn every button inside it red; you write it on each button. This is deliberate: a container that silently recolored everything inside it would turn a red danger zone's Cancel button red too.

`.neutral` names the default explicitly. You rarely need it, because no intent class already means neutral; it matters where color would otherwise come from elsewhere, such as a table row, which inherits its table's intent.

## Presentation: how much color

The Cancel button is `.ghost`: no fill, just colored text, so it reads as less important than Save. That is the presentation axis, two independent choices:

- **Fill:** `.solid` fills the component with its intent color and switches the text to the contrasting color. `.soft` mixes in a light 12% tint and keeps the text in the intent color. `.ghost` has no fill at rest.
- **Edge:** `.edged` draws a border in the intent color; `.edgeless` draws none.

```html
<button class="btn primary">Save changes</button>
<button class="btn primary soft">Preview</button>
<button class="btn primary ghost edged">Export data</button>
<button class="btn ghost">Cancel</button>
```

Every component has its own default when no presentation class applies. A button is solid with no border. A card has no fill and a border. A form field has no fill and a border. [Composing](docs/usage/composing.md#component-defaults) lists the default of every component.

Unlike intent, presentation passes down. A `.soft` on a container makes everything inside it soft unless an element says otherwise, and a class on the element itself always beats one inherited from a container:

```html
<div class="cluster soft">
  <button class="btn primary">Soft primary</button>
  <button class="btn success">Soft success</button>
  <button class="btn primary solid">Solid: its own class wins</button>
</div>
```

Some components limit what presentation can do, to protect something they need. A form field inherited into a `.solid` container fills to only 6%, so typed text stays readable. A checkbox always keeps its border, because the border is the only thing that shows an unchecked box. These limits are listed with each component and collected in [Composing](docs/usage/composing.md).

## Finish the first screen

Add a plan summary next to a usage card in a grid, and give the summary a soft primary tint so it stands out as the account's current state:

```html
<main class="section">
  <div class="section-content narrow stack loose">
    <header class="stack tight">
      <h1 class="text-title">Account settings</h1>
      <p>Manage your profile, plan, and security.</p>
    </header>

    <section class="card stack" aria-labelledby="profile-title">
      <h2 class="text-title-sm" id="profile-title">Profile</h2>
      <p>Your name appears on invoices and shared projects.</p>
      <div class="cluster">
        <button class="btn primary" type="button">Save changes</button>
        <button class="btn ghost" type="button">Cancel</button>
      </div>
    </section>

    <div class="auto-grid">
      <section class="card soft primary stack tight" aria-labelledby="plan-title">
        <h2 class="text-label" id="plan-title">Current plan</h2>
        <p class="text-title-sm">Team, billed yearly</p>
        <p class="text-body">Renews on 12 March 2027.</p>
      </section>
      <section class="card stack tight" aria-labelledby="usage-title">
        <h2 class="text-label" id="usage-title">Storage</h2>
        <p class="text-title-sm">48 GB of 100 GB</p>
        <p class="text-body">Shared by 6 members.</p>
      </section>
    </div>
  </div>
</main>
```

On a wide window the two cards sit side by side; when the column is too narrow for two 16rem columns and the gap between them, they stack. The [Feedback](docs/usage/feedback.md) page turns the storage card's number into a usage bar.

A `.card` rests at one unit of depth, but on the base look that depth has no visible shadow; it appears when an aesthetic draws one or when you add `.raised` or `.floating`. [Composing → Elevation](docs/usage/composing.md#elevation) covers depth.

## Aesthetic: what it is made of

The third axis changes the material of everything inside it: corners, border width, shadows, and sometimes the font. It needs its own import (see [Setup → Add an aesthetic](docs/setup.md#add-an-aesthetic-optional)):

```html
<main class="section neobrutalism">
  <!-- The same settings screen: square corners, thick dark lines, hard offset shadows -->
</main>
```

Like presentation, an aesthetic passes down, and a component inside it can carry a different one. You do not need it to build the screen; [Aesthetics](docs/usage/aesthetics.md) compares all six.

## Words these docs use

Some pages describe how a component is painted. These words have one meaning each:

| Word      | Meaning                                                                                                                                                          |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Fill      | How much of the intent color covers the component, from 0% (`.ghost`) to 100% (`.solid`).                                                                        |
| Cap       | The highest fill a component allows. A form field caps an inherited fill at 6%, for example.                                                                     |
| Plate     | The component's painted background: the fill, mixed over the ground.                                                                                             |
| Ground    | The color the fill is mixed over. Usually the page itself shows through; a few components set their own, such as the light intent tint under `.kbd` and `.code`. |
| Edge      | The border around the component. It is separate from rules, the lines inside a table.                                                                            |
| Ink       | A color used to draw lines: the edge, a table's rules, a checkbox's mark. "Text ink" means the color of text printed on a plate.                                 |
| Material  | What an aesthetic changes: corner radius and shape, border width and style, shadow, and transparency.                                                            |
| Slab      | A hard, unblurred shadow offset down and to one side, as `.neobrutalism` and `.chunky-tile` draw.                                                                |
| Elevation | How much of the shadow in scope an element takes: none (`.flat`), one unit (`.raised`), or two (`.floating`).                                                    |

## Tokens behind the classes

Every class reads CSS custom properties, called tokens, so you can change the result without rewriting a class:

| Kind         | Controls                                                                        | Where it is listed                                                              |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Color        | The palette: intent colors, text, borders, and backgrounds, for light and dark. | [Theming → Color tokens](docs/usage/theming.md#color-tokens)                       |
| Foundation   | Layout widths and gaps, corner radii, control height, focus, motion.            | [Theming → Foundation tokens](docs/usage/theming.md#foundation-tokens)             |
| Intent       | The color slots a component reads after an intent class picks a role.           | [Theming → Intent tokens](docs/usage/theming.md#intent-tokens)                     |
| Presentation | The fill and border percentages the presentation classes set.                   | [Customizing → Presentation tokens](docs/usage/customizing.md#presentation-tokens) |
| Material     | Radius, border width, shadow geometry, and transparency.                        | [Customizing → Material tokens](docs/usage/customizing.md#material-tokens)         |
| Aesthetic    | One knob per aesthetic, such as `--pixel-unit` or `--tile-lift`.                | [Customizing → Aesthetic tokens](docs/usage/customizing.md#aesthetic-tokens)       |

Color and foundation tokens are what most apps change first, to match a brand. The rest are lower level: components read them, and the presentation and aesthetic classes set them for you.

## Limits to know now

- **Intent does not pass down.** Write it on each element that shows it. The only exception is table rows.
- **Classes are styling only.** `<div class="btn">` looks like a button but cannot be focused or pressed with a keyboard. Use `<button>` or `<a href>`, and see [Accessibility](docs/accessibility.md).
- **A combination the docs do not describe is not supported.** It may render, but it can change in any release; see [Introduction → What counts as supported](docs/index.md#what-counts-as-supported).

## Next

The screen has one primary action and one quiet one. [Buttons](docs/usage/buttons.md) adds the rest: a destructive action for the danger zone, icon buttons, sizes, and disabled states.

<!-- Source: docs/usage/index.md -->

# Usage

These guides finish the settings screen started in [Building a screen](docs/concepts.md). Read the first seven in order: each one adds a part of the screen and assumes the ones before it. The next three are lookup pages; you will be sent to them when a guide needs the full table, and you can come back whenever you need a default or a rule. The last page, Presets, is for when the screen works and you are tired of typing the same classes.

Guides, in order:

1. [Buttons](docs/usage/buttons.md): the danger zone's destructive action, icon buttons, sizes, link buttons, and disabled states, plus how to load icons.
2. [Forms](docs/usage/forms.md): the profile form, with labels, hints, validation errors, an input with an icon or a fixed prefix, a select, and checkbox, radio, and switch toggles.
3. [Feedback](docs/usage/feedback.md): what the screen shows while saving and after: a loading button, a success alert, a plan badge, a loading placeholder, and a storage usage bar.
4. [Tooltips](docs/usage/tooltips.md): help text beside a form field, how to wire it for keyboard and screen reader users, and where a tooltip can be cut off.
5. [Theming](docs/usage/theming.md): light and dark mode, replacing the palette with brand colors, and defining an intent of your own, with the full color and foundation token tables.
6. [Aesthetics](docs/usage/aesthetics.md): the six optional looks, what each one changes, and its limits.
7. [Solo classes](docs/usage/solo.md): painting an aesthetic onto a component from another library.

Lookup pages:

- [Composing](docs/usage/composing.md): the complete rules for combining intent, presentation, and elevation, every component's defaults, and which axes each component reads.
- [Customizing](docs/usage/customizing.md): presentation and material tokens, aesthetic knobs, the public component variables, the generated palette, and the composition helpers for building your own components.
- [Content and layout](docs/usage/content-and-layout.md): every layout helper, the type scale, cards and panels, tables, quotes, code, and keyboard keys.

Once the screen works:

- [Presets](docs/usage/presets.md): set a look once, with axis classes on a container, theme and material tokens, or your own component classes built with `@apply`.

When you finish, [Accessibility](docs/accessibility.md) collects what the CSS does for you and what your application still owes its users.

<!-- Source: docs/usage/buttons.md -->

# Buttons

The settings screen has a Save button and a Cancel button. This page adds the rest of its actions: a danger zone with a destructive Delete button, an icon button that copies an API key, and smaller buttons for a dense row. It also covers disabled buttons and how to load the icons used here and on later pages.

## Add a danger zone

A destructive action goes in its own card at the bottom of the screen. The card is soft and destructive so it reads as a warning; the button is solid so it is the loudest thing in that card:

```html
<section class="card soft destructive stack" aria-labelledby="danger-title">
  <h2 class="text-title-sm" id="danger-title">Delete account</h2>
  <p>This removes your projects, invoices, and API keys. It cannot be undone.</p>
  <div class="cluster">
    <button class="btn destructive" type="button">Delete account</button>
    <button class="btn ghost" type="button">Export data first</button>
  </div>
</section>
```

The card and the button each name `.destructive`, because [intent does not pass down](docs/concepts.md#intent-which-color). The Export button keeps its neutral color inside the red card for the same reason.

## Choose a fill and an edge

A button accepts one intent, one fill class, and one edge class, all optional. With none, a button is solid and edgeless:

```html
<button class="btn primary">Save changes</button>
<button class="btn secondary">Preview</button>
<button class="btn primary soft">Invite member</button>
<button class="btn destructive ghost edged">Revoke key</button>
<button class="btn ghost">Cancel</button>
```

A **neutral** button never fills completely. Its color is the page's own text color, so a full fill would be a black or white block, the loudest thing on the page for the intent that means nothing in particular. A neutral `.solid` button stops at a 20% fill instead, a quiet gray a step darker than `.soft`. Every named intent fills to 100%.

On hover, a button's fill deepens by `--hover-step` (14%), so a `.ghost` button picks up a tint and a `.solid` one changes to its intent's hover color. On press it scales down slightly (`scale(0.97)`); an [aesthetic](docs/usage/aesthetics.md) can replace that with its own press, and under a user's reduced-motion preference it still happens, at once.

A neutral `.soft` or `.ghost` button inside a filled surface, such as a Cancel button in a `.card.solid.primary` or an `.alert.solid.destructive`, prints its label and its line in that surface's text color, so it stays readable on the fill. A text field does the same. A button with an intent keeps its own color, and so does a neutral `.solid` one, which rests on a fill of its own.

When a filled button has keyboard focus, a 2px line of the page color runs inside the focus ring, so the ring stays visible on a button filled with the same color, such as `.solid.primary`.

## Sizes and shapes

| Class   | Effect                                                                                                                                       |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| _none_  | At least 2.5rem tall (`--control-height`), 1rem side padding, and the same font size as the surrounding text.                                |
| `.sm`   | At least 2rem tall, 0.75rem side padding, 0.875rem text.                                                                                     |
| `.lg`   | At least 3rem tall, 1.25rem side padding, 1.0625rem text.                                                                                    |
| `.pill` | Fully rounded ends.                                                                                                                          |
| `.icon` | Square. At least 2.5rem on each side, 2rem with `.sm`, 3rem with `.lg`.                                                                      |
| `.p-xs` | Tightest padding (0.5rem sides, 0.125rem top and bottom). Also removes the minimum height, so a button fits a table cell or a dense toolbar. |
| `.p-sm` | Compact padding (0.625rem sides, 0.25rem top and bottom).                                                                                    |
| `.p-lg` | Roomy padding (1.5rem sides, 0.75rem top and bottom).                                                                                        |

A size class and a padding class can be combined. Only `.p-xs` removes the minimum height of a labeled button; every other combination keeps it. On an icon button, any `.p-*` class removes the minimum size and the button sizes to its icon plus that padding: 0.125rem, 0.25rem, or 0.75rem around it.

The base look draws corners that scale with the size: a `.sm` or `.p-sm` button has slightly smaller corners than a default one, and `.lg` slightly larger.

## Icon buttons

The API keys list on the settings screen has a copy button beside each key. An icon-only button needs an accessible name, because the icon has no text a screen reader can read:

```html
<button class="btn icon ghost" type="button" aria-label="Copy API key">
  <i class="ic-lucide-copy" aria-hidden="true"></i>
</button>
<button class="btn ghost sm" type="button">
  <i class="ic-lucide-download" aria-hidden="true"></i>
  Download invoice
</button>
```

A button is a flex row with a 0.5rem gap, so an icon next to a label is spaced without extra markup.

### Loading icons

This package ships no icons. The examples in these docs use `@codenhub/icons` with the Lucide family, and its class names are always written with the family, as `ic-lucide-copy`. Install it and load it once, next to this package:

```sh
pnpm add @codenhub/icons
```

With compiled CSS, import the base rules and each family you use:

```css
@import "@codenhub/styles";
@import "@codenhub/icons";
@import "@codenhub/icons/lucide";
```

With Tailwind source, import its Tailwind entrypoint after this package's:

```css
@import "@codenhub/styles/tw";
@import "@codenhub/icons/tw";
```

Any other icon works too: an inline `<svg>` with `stroke="currentColor"` or `fill="currentColor"` takes the button's text color the same way.

## Links that look like buttons

A link that navigates, such as "View billing history", is still a link. Write it as `<a href>` with `.btn`, and it gets the same look:

```html
<a class="btn secondary ghost edged" href="/settings/billing">View billing history</a>
```

Do not use `<div class="btn">` or `<span class="btn">`: they look like buttons but cannot be focused or activated from a keyboard. Use `<button>` for actions and `<a href>` for navigation.

## Disabled buttons

Any of these makes a button look disabled: the `disabled` attribute, `.disabled`, `aria-disabled="true"`, or `data-disabled`. A disabled button is drawn at 58% opacity with a not-allowed cursor, and does not change on hover or press.

```html
<button class="btn primary" type="submit" disabled>Save changes</button>

<a class="btn ghost" aria-disabled="true">Download invoice</a>
```

Only the `disabled` attribute stops the button from working. `.disabled`, `aria-disabled`, and `data-disabled` change the look only: a click or the Enter key still activates it, so your code has to ignore it. `aria-disabled` is the right choice when the button should stay focusable, for example so a tooltip can explain why it is disabled. A link has no `disabled` attribute, so remove its `href` as well when it should not navigate.

## Loading state

There is no loading class. A loading button is a disabled button with a spinner icon you bring, which [Feedback](docs/usage/feedback.md#show-that-the-form-is-saving) builds for the Save button. Disable it so a second click cannot submit twice.

## Next

The buttons are ready; the card they save has nothing to save yet. [Forms](docs/usage/forms.md) adds the profile fields.

<!-- Source: docs/usage/forms.md -->

# Forms

The profile card has a Save button but nothing to save. This page fills it in: a display name with a hint, an email address that shows a validation error, a profile address with a fixed prefix, a language select, and the toggles for notifications, billing, and profile visibility. The package styles each control; your HTML provides the labels, the validation, and the error messages, and this page shows how to connect them.

## A labeled field

A field is a label, a control, and an optional hint, stacked:

```html
<div class="field">
  <label class="label" for="display-name">Display name</label>
  <input class="ipt" id="display-name" name="display-name" aria-describedby="display-name-hint" />
  <span class="hint" id="display-name-hint">Shown on invoices and shared projects.</span>
</div>
```

- `.field` stacks its children with a small gap (0.35rem) and takes the full width.
- `.label` sets label text: 1rem, medium weight.
- `.hint` is smaller, secondary-colored helper text. Keep it outside the `<label>` and point `aria-describedby` at it, so a screen reader announces it as a description instead of reading it as part of the field's name.
- `.ipt` styles an `<input>`. Use `.textarea` for a `<textarea>` and `.select` for a `<select>`.

A text control is at least 2.5rem tall (`--control-height`), the same height as a default button, so a field and a button line up in a row. Its default look is no fill and a border. A `.textarea` is at least 7rem tall and can be resized vertically.

### Sizes

`.ipt`, `.select`, `.textarea`, and `.input-group` take the button's size classes, so a small field and a small button line up in a row:

| Class   | Height | Side padding | Text      |
| ------- | ------ | ------------ | --------- |
| `.sm`   | 2rem   | 0.625rem     | 0.875rem  |
| default | 2.5rem | 0.75rem      | inherited |
| `.lg`   | 3rem   | 1rem         | 1.0625rem |

The corners scale with the size, as a button's do. A `.textarea` keeps its 7rem minimum height at every size; the class changes its text, padding, and corners. Size an `.input-group` on the group, not on the control inside it: the control and its adornments take the group's text size.

```html
<div class="cluster tight">
  <input class="ipt sm" aria-label="Coupon code" />
  <button class="btn sm" type="button">Apply</button>
</div>
```

## Show a validation error

Mark the control invalid with `aria-invalid="true"` and give the error message `.hint.destructive`:

```html
<div class="field">
  <label class="label" for="email">Email</label>
  <input class="ipt" type="email" id="email" name="email" value="ada@" aria-invalid="true" aria-describedby="email-error" />
  <span class="hint destructive" id="email-error">Enter a full email address, such as ada@example.com.</span>
</div>
```

An invalid control draws its border, focus ring, and typed text in the destructive color, whatever intent class it has. The text uses the readable tone of that color, `--intent-strong`, so it stays legible on the page. The package only paints the state: deciding that the value is invalid, setting and clearing `aria-invalid`, and writing the message are your code. Remove `aria-invalid` once the value is valid again; leaving it set keeps the field red. On a checkbox, radio, or switch, `aria-invalid="true"` draws the toggle exactly as `.destructive` does, checked mark included.

A hint takes any of the six built-in intents, not only `.destructive`: `.hint.success` confirms a value was accepted, and `.hint.warning` flags one that is allowed but unusual. Each prints in its intent's readable tone, `--intent-strong`, which holds 4.5:1 against the page in both themes. A hint with no intent, with `.neutral`, or with an [intent you defined yourself](docs/usage/theming.md#your-own-intent), stays secondary-colored. Only a class on the hint itself colors it; an intent on the field or a container around it does not.

```html
<input class="ipt success" id="username" value="ada" aria-describedby="username-hint" /> <span class="hint success" id="username-hint">That username is available.</span>
```

## Put the profile form together

```html
<form class="card stack" aria-labelledby="profile-title">
  <h2 class="text-title-sm" id="profile-title">Profile</h2>

  <div class="field">
    <label class="label" for="display-name">Display name</label>
    <input class="ipt" id="display-name" name="display-name" value="Ada Lovelace" aria-describedby="display-name-hint" />
    <span class="hint" id="display-name-hint">Shown on invoices and shared projects.</span>
  </div>

  <div class="field">
    <label class="label" for="email">Email</label>
    <input class="ipt" type="email" id="email" name="email" value="ada@example.com" />
  </div>

  <div class="field">
    <label class="label" for="bio">Bio</label>
    <textarea class="textarea" id="bio" name="bio" rows="3"></textarea>
  </div>

  <div class="field">
    <label class="label" for="language">Language</label>
    <select class="select" id="language" name="language">
      <option>English</option>
      <option>Português</option>
      <option>Español</option>
    </select>
  </div>

  <div class="cluster">
    <button class="btn primary" type="submit">Save changes</button>
    <button class="btn ghost" type="reset">Cancel</button>
  </div>
</form>
```

A `.select` draws its own arrow. With `multiple` or a `size` above 1 it becomes a list box instead: no arrow, as tall as the rows it shows. The open list of options is drawn by the browser and the operating system, so it does not take the package's look.

## Add an icon or a fixed prefix

`.input-group` puts an icon or a piece of text inside a field's border. The group draws the border, background, focus ring, and invalid and disabled states; the control inside it gives up its own, so the border is drawn once. Place the adornment before the control to put it at the start, after it to put it at the end. A group is the height of a lone field, so it lines up with the fields and buttons beside it.

The profile address always starts with the same host, so it is a fixed prefix:

```html
<div class="field">
  <label class="label" for="profile-url">Profile address</label>
  <div class="input-group" style="--input-group-gap: 0">
    <span>app.example.com/u/</span>
    <input class="ipt" id="profile-url" name="profile-url" value="ada" />
  </div>
</div>
```

The gap between the control and its adornment is `--input-group-gap`, 0.5rem by default. That suits an icon, but text meant to read as part of the value looks broken with a space after it, so the example sets it to `0`. Set it on the group, or once on a form for every group in it. It is one of the [public component variables](docs/usage/customizing.md#component-variables).

A members search, with an icon at the start (the `ic-lucide-*` classes need `@codenhub/icons` loaded; see [Buttons → Loading icons](docs/usage/buttons.md#loading-icons)):

```html
<div class="field">
  <label class="label" for="member-search">Find a member</label>
  <div class="input-group">
    <i class="ic-lucide-search" aria-hidden="true"></i>
    <input class="ipt" type="search" id="member-search" name="q" />
  </div>
</div>
```

A `.select` works in a group too. The group removes the control's side padding, except at the end of a single-row select, which keeps 1.75rem so the chosen option's text does not run under the arrow.

Any element works as the adornment: an icon class, an inline `<svg>`, an `<img>`, or text. The package ships no icons for fields, because a built-in image could not follow your text color, theme, or aesthetic.

The group reads intent and presentation the way a lone `.ipt` does: `.input-group.primary` colors the border and the typed text, and `.input-group.soft.edgeless` is a field sunk into the page. Put the intent on the group, not on the control inside: the group draws the field, so the control's text takes the group's intent and an intent class on the control has no effect. `aria-invalid="true"` or `disabled` on the control inside applies to the whole group, and so does either on the group itself. The group's focus ring appears when its field has focus, so unlike a lone field it also shows after a mouse click. A button inside the group, such as a clear button, draws its own ring when it has focus, and the group draws none: one ring always marks the one control that has focus.

## Browser decorations

Some input types come with built-in buttons: a date or time field's picker button, a number field's up and down arrows, and a search field's clear button. The package keeps them, because each one also does something: the picker button is the only way to open the picker with a mouse, and the clear button empties the field.

`.unadorned` removes them, for a field where you draw your own. Put it on the control, or on its `.input-group`. Removing a decoration removes what it did, so connect your replacement yourself: `input.showPicker()` opens a picker, `stepUp()` and `stepDown()` replace the arrows, and setting `value` to `""` and dispatching an `input` event replaces a clear button. Typing keeps working either way. Firefox gives no way to remove its date picker button, so it stays there.

```html
<div class="field">
  <label class="label" for="member-filter">Find a member</label>
  <div class="input-group unadorned">
    <i class="ic-lucide-search" aria-hidden="true"></i>
    <input class="ipt" type="search" id="member-filter" name="q" />
    <button class="btn icon ghost p-xs" type="button" aria-label="Clear search">
      <i class="ic-lucide-x" aria-hidden="true"></i>
    </button>
  </div>
</div>
```

The clear button above is a real `<button>` with an accessible name. A button inside a group keeps its own classes: a `.btn.ghost` has no fill and, like every button by default, no border, so it sits inside the field's border without drawing one of its own.

## Toggles

The settings screen has three kinds of toggle: a checkbox to opt into invoice emails, radio buttons to choose a billing period, and a switch to make the profile public. Each class goes on a native `<input>` of the matching type:

```html
<fieldset class="stack tight">
  <legend class="label">Notifications</legend>
  <label class="cluster tight">
    <input class="checkbox" type="checkbox" name="invoice-email" checked />
    Email me when an invoice is ready
  </label>
</fieldset>

<fieldset class="stack tight">
  <legend class="label">Billing period</legend>
  <label class="cluster tight">
    <input class="radio" type="radio" name="period" value="monthly" />
    Monthly
  </label>
  <label class="cluster tight">
    <input class="radio" type="radio" name="period" value="yearly" checked />
    Yearly, two months free
  </label>
</fieldset>

<label class="cluster tight">
  <input class="switch primary" type="checkbox" role="switch" name="public-profile" />
  Public profile
</label>
```

- `.checkbox` goes on `type="checkbox"`, `.radio` on `type="radio"`, and `.switch` on `type="checkbox"`. Give a switch `role="switch"` yourself, so it is announced as on or off rather than checked.
- `.cluster.tight` on the `<label>` lines the control up with its text and leaves a 0.5rem gap.
- A checkbox whose `indeterminate` property is set, for a group where only some items are checked, shows a dash, and keeps the dash while also `checked`, as the browser's own checkbox does. Set it from script (`input.indeterminate = true`); there is no attribute for it.

### Checked and unchecked colors

An intent class sets the checked color. With no intent, a checked toggle is filled with the text color, and the mark is drawn in the page color: a black box with a white check on a light page. Unlike a neutral button, a neutral toggle fills all the way when checked.

Presentation changes only the unchecked look. Every toggle rests at `.soft`; once checked, each has one look whatever its presentation:

| Toggle           | Unchecked fill | Checked                                        |
| ---------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `.ghost`         | 0%             | 100% fill, with the mark in the contrast color |
| `.soft`, default | 12%            | 100% fill, with the mark in the contrast color |
| `.solid`         | 40%            | 100% fill, with the mark in the contrast color |

A checked checkbox and a checked switch cut their mark out of the filled plate. A checked radio thickens its ring to twice the resting line width, up to 3px, takes the full intent color on it, and shows a dot. The 3px limit keeps the ring from swallowing the dot under an aesthetic with a thick line.

`.checkbox` and `.radio` always draw their border, even with `.edgeless`, because the border is the only thing that shows an unchecked box. `.switch.ghost` keeps its border too, since with no fill and no border nothing would mark the track. These are listed in [Composing](docs/usage/composing.md#component-axis-reference).

An aesthetic that draws its border as an inner shadow, such as `.pixel`, cannot make that shadow wider than the toggle's border width. A 16px checkbox or a 20px switch has no room for a thicker inner ring without covering the mark. This only matters if you set `--ui-shadow-spread` yourself; see [Customizing → Material tokens](docs/usage/customizing.md#material-tokens).

## Fill and border on text controls

Text controls take intent, which colors the border, the focus ring, and the typed text, the text in the intent's readable tone (`--intent-strong`). They also take both presentation axes. Their fill is capped low, so typed text stays readable:

| On a text control                               | Fill |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ---- |
| `.ghost`, default                               | 0%   |
| Any fill from a container (`.soft` or `.solid`) | 6%   |
| `.soft` on the control                          | 12%  |
| `.solid` on the control                         | 20%  |

A container's fill is meant for the surfaces in it, so a field nobody classed takes only a faint 6% of it. Put the class on the field itself for more.

The border works the same way. An `.edgeless` inherited from a container is ignored, so a toolbar cannot leave a field with no visible edge. `.edgeless` written on the control itself is honored: that is how you ask for a borderless field. A borderless field does not meet the WCAG 1.4.11 contrast requirement for a control's boundary, so it is never a default; its focus ring still shows.

```html
<input class="ipt success" placeholder="Matches your current password" />
<input class="ipt soft edged" placeholder="Tinted, with a border" />
<input class="ipt soft edgeless" placeholder="Sunk into the page" />
<div class="soft">
  <input class="ipt" placeholder="A container's .soft gives a 6% tint" />
</div>
```

At rest, a field's border is deliberately lighter than 3:1 against the page, so hover and focus have a visible change to make. [Accessibility → Control boundaries](docs/accessibility.md#control-boundaries) explains the trade-off and how to get a stronger border.

## Disabled controls

`disabled`, `aria-disabled="true"`, `data-disabled`, or `.disabled` on a control draws it at reduced opacity with a not-allowed cursor. As with buttons, only the `disabled` attribute stops input; the others change the look only.

## Building your own control

For a text-like control the package does not ship, `.text-control` gives an element the same border, placeholder, hover, focus, invalid, and disabled styles as `.ipt`, without its height or padding. [Customizing → Composition helpers](docs/usage/customizing.md#composition-helpers) explains it with the other building blocks.

## Next

The form can be filled in and submitted. [Feedback](docs/usage/feedback.md) shows what the screen does next: a Save button that says it is saving, a success message, a plan badge, and a storage usage bar.

<!-- Source: docs/usage/feedback.md -->

# Feedback

The profile form can be submitted, but nothing tells the user what happened. This page adds the screen's feedback: a Save button that shows it is working, an alert when the save succeeds, a badge on the plan card, a placeholder while the profile loads, and bars for storage use and a data export. The package draws each of these; your code decides when they appear, updates their values, and makes sure screen readers hear about them.

## Show that the form is saving

There is no loading class. A saving button is a disabled button with a spinning icon:

```html
<button class="btn primary" type="submit" disabled>
  <i class="ic-lucide-loader-circle ic-anim-spin" aria-hidden="true"></i>
  Saving…
</button>
```

The spinner comes from `@codenhub/icons`, which this package does not load. Load it once, as [Buttons → Loading icons](docs/usage/buttons.md#loading-icons) shows; with compiled CSS that is:

```css
@import "@codenhub/icons";
@import "@codenhub/icons/lucide";
```

`ic-anim-spin` rotates the icon and stops when the user asks the system for reduced motion. The animated `svg-spinners` family in `@codenhub/icons` is different: its artwork keeps moving under that preference. Either icon takes the button's text color.

Disabling the button stops a second click from submitting twice. Whether to keep or replace the label is up to you; the package has no way to hide it. A changing button label is not reliably announced, so tell screen reader users the outcome with a status message, as the next section does.

## Confirm the result with an alert

When the save succeeds, show an alert above the form:

```html
<div class="alert success" role="status">Profile saved.</div>
```

`role="status"` makes screen readers announce the text politely, after what they are reading. For an error the user must act on, use `role="alert"`, which interrupts:

```html
<div class="alert destructive" role="alert">Your changes were not saved. Check your connection and try again.</div>
```

Screen readers announce a live region when its content changes, so render the region empty when the page loads and put the message into it, rather than inserting a new alert element with the text already inside. The package adds no role, timing, or dismiss button; those are yours.

An alert is a row with a 0.75rem gap, so an icon placed before the message is spaced automatically. `.alert-icon` sizes an icon to 1.25rem and aligns it with the first line of text:

```html
<div class="alert warning" role="status">
  <i class="alert-icon ic-lucide-triangle-alert" aria-hidden="true"></i>
  Your card expires next month. Update it to keep your plan.
</div>
```

Any icon element works: a class from an icon set, an inline `<svg>`, or an `<img>`. `@codenhub/icons` sizes its glyphs in a rule no class can outrank, so `.alert-icon` also sets that set's `--ic-size`. To resize an alert icon, write your own rule that sets `width`, `height`, and, for `@codenhub/icons`, `--ic-size`.

### How alerts look

With no presentation class, an alert is soft and edged: a light tint of its intent, intent-colored text, and a border. Presentation classes change that like on any component, such as `.alert.primary.solid` for a filled banner.

An alert with no intent is an exception. It has no tint at rest; it uses `--color-foreground`, the quiet background tone one step off the page, the same as a neutral `.card.soft` or `.panel`. An alert with `.primary`, `.secondary`, `.success`, `.warning`, `.destructive`, or `.info` keeps its tint. Only those six classes count here: an alert with an intent class you defined yourself is treated as having no intent; see [Theming → Your own intent](docs/usage/theming.md#your-own-intent).

## Label the plan with a badge

A badge is a small pill for a status or a count:

```html
<section class="card soft primary stack tight" aria-labelledby="plan-title">
  <div class="cluster between">
    <h2 class="text-label" id="plan-title">Current plan</h2>
    <span class="badge success">Active</span>
  </div>
  <p class="text-title-sm">Team, billed yearly</p>
</section>
```

A badge is soft with no border by default, and takes the same intent and presentation classes as a button: `.badge.warning` for "Payment due", `.badge.info.solid` for a filled "New". Unlike an alert, a badge with no intent keeps its light tint, because it has no border, and without the tint it would disappear into the text around it.

A neutral badge that is not `.solid`, such as a count inside a `.btn.primary`, prints in the text color of the filled component it sits in, so it stays readable on that fill. A badge with an intent keeps its own color.

## Show a placeholder while loading

While the profile card waits for data, show gray blocks where the text will be:

```html
<section class="card stack" aria-busy="true" aria-labelledby="profile-title">
  <h2 class="text-title-sm" id="profile-title">Profile</h2>
  <p class="visually-hidden">Loading your profile…</p>
  <div class="stack tight" aria-hidden="true">
    <div class="skeleton" style="height: 2.5rem"></div>
    <div class="skeleton" style="width: 60%"></div>
  </div>
</section>
```

A `.skeleton` fills the width of its container and is at least 1rem tall. It has no size or shape of its own: use a block element such as a `<div>`, and set its width and height to match the content it stands in for. An empty inline element such as `<span class="skeleton">` has no size and does not appear.

A skeleton takes an intent but ignores presentation. With no intent, it is a light gray tinted by the surrounding text color. It shows a moving shimmer that stops when the user asks for reduced motion.

Mark the blocks `aria-hidden="true"`, because they mean nothing to a screen reader. Say that the content is loading in text instead, as the visually hidden paragraph does, and remove `aria-busy` once the content is in place.

## Show progress

The storage card shows how much space is used, and the danger zone's "Export data first" button starts an export that takes a while. Both are `.progress` bars:

```html
<div class="progress" role="meter" aria-label="Storage used" aria-valuemin="0" aria-valuemax="100" aria-valuenow="48" aria-valuetext="48 GB of 100 GB" style="--progress-value: 48%"></div>

<div class="progress primary" role="progressbar" aria-label="Export progress" aria-valuemin="0" aria-valuemax="100" aria-valuenow="20" style="--progress-value: 20%"></div>
```

`--progress-value` is the width of the filled part, as a percentage of the track. It is 0% when unset.

- **Write it with `%`.** `--progress-value: 48` without a unit is not a valid width, and the bar shows empty.
- **Nothing is clamped or checked.** Above 100%, the fill is cut off at the end of the track and looks full; a negative value is not a valid width either. Keep the value between 0% and 100% in your code.
- **The visual value and the announced value are separate.** The bar's width comes from `--progress-value`; what a screen reader announces comes from `aria-valuenow`. The package does not connect them, so update both together.

```js
function setExportProgress(bar, percent) {
  const value = Math.min(100, Math.max(0, Math.round(percent)));
  bar.classList.remove("indeterminate");
  bar.style.setProperty("--progress-value", `${value}%`);
  bar.setAttribute("aria-valuenow", String(value));
}
```

When you do not know how far along the work is, such as while the export is being prepared, use `.indeterminate`. A bar about a third of the track wide sweeps from start to end, again and again, and `--progress-value` is ignored. Remove `aria-valuenow`, because there is no known value to announce:

```html
<div class="progress primary indeterminate" role="progressbar" aria-label="Preparing export"></div>
```

`.active` adds a shimmer over the track of a determinate bar, to show that work is still happening between updates. Both animations stop when the user asks for reduced motion; an indeterminate bar then rests with its fill at the start.

With the [classless stylesheet](docs/setup.md#classless-html), a plain `<progress>` element is drawn as `.progress`: filled to its `value`, or the indeterminate sweep when it has no `value`. It announces its value itself, so it needs no `aria-valuenow`.

### How progress bars look

The fill is the intent color at full strength, or `currentColor` with no intent. The track is soft and edgeless by default: a light tint with no border.

The default track is faint. Against the page it measures about 1.1:1 to 1.3:1, below the 3:1 that WCAG 1.4.11 asks of the parts of a graphic needed to understand it. When the track's extent matters, use `.ghost.edged` with an intent class, which draws an outline around it in the intent's color. With no intent the outline is a light gray that measures below 3:1; [Accessibility → Progress outlines](docs/accessibility.md#progress-outlines) has the measurements and what to do for a neutral bar. `.solid` is not supported on the track, because the fill and the track would be the same color. `.ghost.edgeless` renders, but leaves the track with no visible frame.

To change the colors of the fill, the track, or its border without changing the intent, set `--progress-color`, `--progress-surface`, or `--progress-edge` on the bar or any element around it. They and `--progress-value` are listed in [Customizing → Component variables](docs/usage/customizing.md#component-variables).

## Animation that keeps running

Skeletons, `.active` shimmers, indeterminate bars, and spinners animate for as long as they are on the page. The package stops its own animations when the user asks the system for reduced motion, but that is not the only requirement. WCAG 2.2.2 asks that motion which starts automatically, lasts more than five seconds, and is shown alongside other content can be paused, stopped, or hidden by the user, unless the motion is essential.

A loading indicator shown while the user cannot do anything else, and that would confuse them if it were missing, counts as essential. A shimmer or spinner that keeps moving next to content the user is working with, such as a decorative "live" shimmer on a card, does not. Remove those as soon as their work is done, or give the user a control that stops them.

## Next

The screen now reports what it is doing. [Tooltips](docs/usage/tooltips.md) adds short help text beside a form field.

<!-- Source: docs/usage/tooltips.md -->

# Tooltips

The "Public profile" switch on the settings screen deserves a short explanation: what becomes visible when it is on. This page adds a help button beside it that shows a tooltip on hover and on keyboard focus. The CSS shows and hides the message and draws it; you connect it to its trigger for screen readers, add the Escape key, and check that nothing around it cuts it off.

## A help tooltip

```html
<div class="cluster tight">
  <label class="cluster tight">
    <input class="switch primary" type="checkbox" role="switch" name="public-profile" />
    Public profile
  </label>
  <span class="tooltip">
    <button class="tooltip-icon" type="button" aria-label="About public profiles" aria-describedby="public-profile-help">?</button>
    <span class="tooltip-bubble" role="tooltip" id="public-profile-help">Anyone with the link can see your name, photo, and public projects.</span>
  </span>
</div>
```

The three parts:

- `.tooltip` wraps the trigger and the message. It positions the message and paints nothing itself.
- `.tooltip-bubble` is the message. It is a real element, so it can have an `id` that the trigger points to.
- `.tooltip-icon` is a small round trigger, for a message with nothing else to attach to. Any focusable element can be the trigger instead: wrap an existing `.btn` in `.tooltip` and it keeps its own look.

Connect them yourself: an `id` on the bubble, `aria-describedby` on the trigger pointing to that `id`, and `role="tooltip"` on the bubble. A screen reader then reads the message as the trigger's description. The CSS cannot make this connection, and without it the message is visual only.

The trigger must be focusable, such as a `<button>`, so keyboard users can reach the message. The bubble opens when anything inside `.tooltip` has focus, so it also opens after a mouse click on the trigger.

## Placement

The bubble opens above its trigger, horizontally centered, with a 0.5rem gap. Set `data-tooltip-position` on `.tooltip` to choose another side:

```html
<span class="tooltip" data-tooltip-position="bottom">
  <button class="btn ghost sm" type="button" aria-describedby="renewal-help">Renews 12 March 2027</button>
  <span class="tooltip-bubble" role="tooltip" id="renewal-help">Your card is charged on this date.</span>
</span>
```

| `data-tooltip-position` | Bubble                                            |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| _none_ or `"top"`       | Above the trigger, centered.                      |
| `"bottom"`              | Below the trigger, centered.                      |
| `"left"`                | To the left of the trigger, centered vertically.  |
| `"right"`               | To the right of the trigger, centered vertically. |

A bubble is as wide as its text, up to 18rem, and then wraps.

### Where a tooltip gets cut off

The bubble is positioned with CSS only, on the side you chose. Nothing measures the page: it does not move to stay inside the window, flip to the other side when there is no room, or move to the top layer of the page. That has three consequences:

- **A scrolling or clipping container cuts it off.** An ancestor with `overflow: hidden`, `auto`, or `scroll` clips the bubble at its edge. The API keys table on the settings screen sits in a `.table-wrap`, which scrolls, so a top tooltip on the first row is cut off at the top of the wrapper. Raising `z-index` does not help: it changes what the bubble is painted above, not whether the container clips it.
- **The window edge cuts it off.** A top tooltip on the first line of a page, or a right tooltip near the right edge, extends off screen.
- **Left and right are physical sides.** In a right-to-left page, `"left"` still means the left side of the screen.

What to do:

- Choose a side with room: on a table's first row, use `data-tooltip-position="bottom"`.
- Move the tooltip's trigger out of the clipping container, or remove the `overflow` from a container that does not need it.
- If the trigger's position cannot be known in advance, such as in a scrolling list or a resizable panel, use a positioning library or your framework's popover component, which can measure and flip. You can still give its message element the `.tooltip-bubble` classes for the look, but the showing, hiding, and positioning described on this page then come from that library, not from `.tooltip`.

## Hover, linger, and Escape

WCAG 1.4.13 asks three things of content that appears on hover or focus. The package handles two:

- **Hoverable.** When the pointer leaves the trigger, the bubble stays for `--tooltip-linger` (300ms) and then fades, so the pointer can cross the gap onto it. It stays open while the pointer is over it. A closed bubble is `visibility: hidden`, so it never catches the pointer.
- **Persistent.** It stays open until the pointer and focus leave.
- **Dismissible.** The user must be able to close it without moving the pointer or focus, usually with Escape. CSS cannot listen for a key, so this part is yours.

To change the linger time, set `--tooltip-linger` on the `.tooltip` element or on any element around it, for example `style="--tooltip-linger: 500ms"`. Keep it long enough for the pointer to reach the bubble. `--tooltip-gap` sets the space between the trigger the same way. Both are [public component variables](docs/usage/customizing.md#component-variables).

For Escape, write `data-state="closed"` on `.tooltip`: it hides the bubble even while it is hovered or focused. Remove the attribute only when both the pointer and focus have left the tooltip, so the next hover or focus opens it again. Removing it earlier, while the trigger still has focus, makes the message reappear without the user doing anything.

```js
for (const tooltip of document.querySelectorAll(".tooltip")) {
  let pointerInside = tooltip.matches(":hover");

  tooltip.addEventListener("pointerenter", () => {
    pointerInside = true;
  });

  tooltip.addEventListener("pointerleave", () => {
    pointerInside = false;
    if (!tooltip.contains(document.activeElement)) tooltip.removeAttribute("data-state");
  });

  tooltip.addEventListener("focusout", (event) => {
    const focusStaysInside = tooltip.contains(event.relatedTarget);
    if (!focusStaysInside && !pointerInside) tooltip.removeAttribute("data-state");
  });
}

document.addEventListener("keydown", (event) => {
  if (event.key !== "Escape") return;
  for (const tooltip of document.querySelectorAll(".tooltip:hover, .tooltip:focus-within")) {
    tooltip.dataset.state = "closed";
  }
});
```

`data-state="open"` does the opposite: it shows the bubble with no hover or focus, for a message that should stay visible, or for a test or a screenshot.

## How the bubble looks

With no intent class, the bubble uses `--color-tooltip`, a background chosen per theme: near-white on a light page, mid gray on a dark one, with `--color-tooltip-contrast` as its text color. Near-white measures only 1.04:1 against a light page, so the bubble also draws a thin border, and a container's `.edgeless` cannot remove it. `.edgeless` on the bubble itself still can. The background stays opaque under any presentation, so the bubble stays readable over whatever it covers.

An intent class fills the bubble with that intent's color and switches the text to the matching contrast color:

- `.tooltip-bubble.primary` has a near-black background with near-white text on a light page, and a near-white background with near-black text on a dark one.
- `.tooltip-bubble.destructive` has a red background with light text in both themes.

Put intent, presentation, aesthetic, and elevation classes on `.tooltip-bubble`, the element that is painted, not on `.tooltip`. The bubble is flat by default, even under an aesthetic that draws depth; add `.raised` or `.floating` to the bubble to lift it. An aesthetic in scope shapes the bubble like any other component; under `.glass` it is frosted like a card. `.tooltip-icon` takes the aesthetic's corner: square under `.neobrutalism` and `.pixel`, a diamond under `.cyber`.

The bubble appears without scaling up when the user asks for reduced motion.

## Next

The settings screen is complete in its default look. [Theming](docs/usage/theming.md) gives it a dark mode and your brand colors.

<!-- Source: docs/usage/theming.md -->

# Theming

The settings screen works and looks like the package's defaults: near-black actions on a near-white page. This page makes it yours. It covers light and dark mode, then replaces the primary color with a brand color in both modes, then defines an intent the package does not ship. The second half is the lookup reference: every color, intent, foundation, and font token, with its default.

## Light and dark

Out of the box, the page follows the operating system: light when the user's system is light, dark when it is dark. You do nothing for that.

To let the user choose, put a theme selector on the root element:

```html
<html data-theme="dark">
  …
</html>
```

| Theme | Equivalent selectors                             |
| ----- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Light | `.light`, `.theme-light`, `[data-theme="light"]` |
| Dark  | `.dark`, `.theme-dark`, `[data-theme="dark"]`    |

A settings screen with a "System / Light / Dark" choice removes the attribute for System and sets it for the other two.

How it resolves:

- A theme selector sets the CSS `color-scheme` property, and the element's text color to `--color-text`. Every color token holds its light and its dark value at once, through `light-dark()`, and the element's `color-scheme` picks one.
- `color-scheme` inherits, so a selector themes everything inside it. A selector on any element themes that part of the page: a dark sidebar on a light page is `<aside class="dark">`, and the text inside it takes the dark theme's text color.
- A selector sets no background. Give the region its ground yourself, such as `background: var(--color-background)`. Any utility or component class on the same element overrides the selector's text color.
- The nearest selector wins, at any depth. A `.light` card inside a `.dark` page is light.
- With no selector, the root has `color-scheme: light dark`, which follows the system.
- Put one theme on an element. If an element carries both a light and a dark selector, dark wins, but do not rely on that.
- Setting `color-scheme` yourself on an element themes the tokens the same way, because it is the only thing the palette reads. It also themes native parts such as scrollbars and the inside of form controls. Plain text inside keeps the color it inherited until you also set `color: var(--color-text)`.

Every component color comes from a token or from `currentColor`, so components follow the theme with no dark-mode rules of their own. The marks the package draws, such as the checkbox tick and the select arrow, use `currentColor` too. Icons and images you add are yours to theme.

`light-dark()` works from Chrome 123, Safari 17.5, and Firefox 120. The package as a whole needs Firefox 128; see [Setup → Requirements](docs/setup.md#requirements).

### Printing

A page prints in the light theme, whatever theme it shows on screen. Under `@media print`, the root and every dark selector set `color-scheme: light`, so every token resolves to its light value, a forced-dark sidebar's included. Paper is light, and dark text on it costs less ink than a printed dark page.

Filled components print their background. A browser drops backgrounds from a printed page by default, which leaves a solid button's contrast text on nothing, so every component sets `print-color-adjust: exact`. The property inherits, so the content inside a component keeps its colors too.

One limit: a `dark:` utility still applies in print. It matches by selector, not by `color-scheme`, so `<html class="dark">` with `dark:bg-black` on an element prints that background black. Write a `print:` utility beside it if the printed page matters.

### The `dark:` variant

With the Tailwind source entrypoints (`/tw`), the package replaces Tailwind's `dark:` variant so your own utilities follow the same theme as the tokens. A `dark:` utility applies under an explicit dark selector on the element or an ancestor, or under a dark system preference when no ancestor sets a theme:

```html
<html>
  <body>
    <p class="dark:text-white">Follows the system preference</p>
    <div class="light">
      <p class="dark:text-white">Stays light: this part of the page chose a theme</p>
    </div>
  </body>
</html>
```

It differs from the tokens in one case: an explicit theme nested inside the opposite one. A `.light` element inside a `.dark` one has light tokens, because the nearest `color-scheme` wins. But `dark:` matches by selector, and `.dark *` matches every element inside `.dark`, so a `dark:` utility inside that `.light` element still applies. If a page uses both tokens and `dark:` utilities, do not nest opposite themes.

The compiled entrypoints do not define a `dark:` variant; they have no Tailwind build to define it in. The [`chs build` command](docs/integrating/without-a-bundler.md#variants) does offer `dark:`, with the same selectors, on the intent, presentation, and modifier classes only.

## Change the brand color

The primary color is near-black on a light page and near-white on a dark one. To make it a brand color, replace the whole primary family: the base color and its four companions. Each holds a light and a dark value:

```css
:root {
  --color-primary: light-dark(#0f766e, #2dd4bf);
  --color-primary-contrast: light-dark(#ffffff, #042f2e);
  --color-primary-hover: light-dark(#115e59, #5eead4);
  --color-primary-subtle: light-dark(#ccfbf1, #134e4a);
  --color-primary-strong: light-dark(#115e59, #5eead4);
}
```

What each one is for:

| Token                      | Role                                                                   | Check                                          |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `--color-primary`          | The fill of a solid primary button, a checked toggle, a progress fill. | Text in `-contrast` on it reaches 4.5:1.       |
| `--color-primary-contrast` | Text and icons on a full primary fill.                                 | See above.                                     |
| `--color-primary-hover`    | The fill under the pointer.                                            | Text in `-contrast` on it still reaches 4.5:1. |
| `--color-primary-subtle`   | The light tint behind soft components.                                 | Text in `-strong` on it reaches 4.5:1.         |
| `--color-primary-strong`   | Text, icons, and borders where the fill is not full: soft and ghost.   | Reaches 4.5:1 on the page and on `-subtle`.    |

The teal values above measure, in light and dark mode: 5.47:1 and 7.77:1 for the fill and its text, 7.27:1 and 13.38:1 for the strong tone on the page, and 6.73:1 and 6.41:1 for the strong tone on the subtle tint.

Replace the whole family. Changing only `--color-primary` leaves its companions on the old near-black, so a soft primary badge keeps gray text and a hovered button flashes black. The focus ring is drawn from `--color-primary` at 64% opacity, so it follows the brand color without a change of its own.

The same pattern works for every family in [Color tokens](#color-tokens): `--color-accent` is what `.secondary` reads, and the four status families are `success`, `warning`, `destructive`, and `info`. Set them on `:root` for the whole page, or on any element to retheme only what is inside it.

The values must be complete colors: hex, `rgb()`, `oklch()`, or a variable you declared yourself. Tailwind palette variables such as `--color-teal-700` exist in a `/tw` build, from your Tailwind theme, but the compiled CSS declares only the palette colors the package itself uses. With compiled CSS, a reference to any other palette variable is empty, and the color it feeds is lost.

With `/tw`, you can drop the Tailwind hues your design does not use, so `bg-red-500` and its siblings stop being classes. Keep the ones the theme reads, `neutral`, `emerald`, `amber`, `rose`, `indigo`, and `white`: cleared, the colors built from them are lost without an error. [Tailwind CSS v4 → Drop Tailwind's palette](docs/integrating/tailwind.md#drop-tailwinds-palette) has the block to copy.

## Your own intent

The package ships six intents: `.primary`, `.secondary`, `.success`, `.warning`, `.destructive`, and `.info`, and the default, `.neutral`. To add one, such as a "Beta" color for features in preview, write a class that sets the seven intent slots. Use complete colors, with `light-dark()` for anything that changes between themes:

```css
.beta {
  --intent-color: #7c3aed;
  --intent-contrast: #ffffff;
  --intent-hover: #6d28d9;
  --intent-strong: light-dark(#5b21b6, #c4b5fd);
  --intent-subtle: light-dark(#ede9fe, #4c1d95);
  --intent-border: light-dark(#7c3aed, #a78bfa);
  --intent-fill-max: 100%;
}
```

```html
<span class="badge beta">Beta</span> <button class="btn beta" type="button">Try the new editor</button>
```

These values measure 5.7:1 for white on the fill, 7.1:1 for white on the hover color, 8.61:1 (light) and 10.72:1 (dark) for the strong tone on the page, and 7.57:1 and 5.93:1 for the strong tone on the subtle tint.

**Set every slot**, including `--intent-fill-max`. Each component resets all seven slots to the neutral values at its own root, so a slot you leave out keeps neutral's value, and without `--intent-fill-max: 100%` your intent fills only to 20%, like neutral. What each slot does is in [Intent tokens](#intent-tokens).

The class works on everything that takes an intent: buttons, badges, fields and toggles, solid and ghost cards, progress bars, skeletons, tooltip bubbles, and the rest. A few behaviors are written for the six built-in names, and a custom intent does not get them:

- **A quiet, untinted rest.** A neutral `.card.soft`, `.panel`, and `.alert` rest on the quiet background tone, and they recognize an intent only by the six built-in classes. `.card.soft.beta`, `.panel.beta`, and `.alert.beta` are drawn like the neutral one: the quiet background tone instead of a violet tint. Your intent still colors their text and border.
- **The chip tint.** A `.beta` key cap or code block shows your `--intent-subtle` tint, but not the extra 12% of `--intent-color` a built-in intent adds over it.
- **Solo classes.** A [solo class](docs/usage/solo.md) such as `.neobrutalism-solo` takes an intent only from the six built-in classes, so `.neobrutalism-solo.beta` is drawn neutral.
- **Hint text.** A [`.hint`](docs/usage/forms.md#show-a-validation-error) prints in an intent's readable tone only for the six built-in classes, so `.hint.beta` stays secondary-colored.
- **Table rows.** A body row recolors its text, line, and hover only for the built-in intent classes. `<tr class="beta">` looks like the rest of its table.

If you need those, there are two ways:

- **Retheme a built-in intent instead.** Set the `--color-info` family (or another one) to your colors, as in [Change the brand color](#change-the-brand-color), and write `.info`. Everything, including the cases above, then works. The cost is that the change reaches every `.info` inside the element you set it on, so set it on the narrowest element that works, and do not do it with an intent the page already uses for its own meaning.
- **Paint it yourself.** Write your own CSS for that one component, such as a `background-color` on `.panel.beta`.

> **Intent does not pass down.** Each component resets the intent slots at its own root, so a `.success` container does not recolor a destructive button inside it. Put the intent class on the element that shows the color.

## Color tokens

Every color token holds a light and a dark value through `light-dark()`; one value means both themes use it. Palette names such as `neutral-950` are Tailwind's default palette, which the package's compiled CSS declares for the colors it uses.

Each row is an override point: set it on `:root` to retheme the page, or on any element to retheme what is inside it. The `-hover`, `-subtle`, `-strong`, and `-contrast` rows are companions of their family's base color and do not follow it, so retheme the whole family. The `text` family has no `-subtle` row: the neutral intent takes its subtle tone from `--color-surface`.

| Token                          | Light, dark                  | Purpose                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--color-primary`              | `neutral-950`, `neutral-50`  | Fill of `.primary`.                                                                            |
| `--color-primary-contrast`     | `neutral-50`, `neutral-950`  | Text and icons on a full primary fill.                                                         |
| `--color-primary-hover`        | `neutral-700`, `neutral-200` | Primary fill under the pointer.                                                                |
| `--color-primary-subtle`       | `neutral-200`, `neutral-900` | Primary tint behind soft components.                                                           |
| `--color-primary-strong`       | `neutral-900`, `neutral-100` | Primary text, icons, and borders where the fill is not full.                                   |
| `--color-accent`               | `neutral-600`, `neutral-400` | Fill of `.secondary`.                                                                          |
| `--color-accent-contrast`      | `neutral-50`, `neutral-950`  | Text and icons on a full secondary fill.                                                       |
| `--color-accent-hover`         | `neutral-700`, `neutral-300` | Secondary fill under the pointer.                                                              |
| `--color-accent-subtle`        | `neutral-100`, `neutral-800` | Secondary tint behind soft components.                                                         |
| `--color-accent-strong`        | `neutral-800`, `neutral-200` | Secondary text, icons, and borders where the fill is not full.                                 |
| `--color-border`               | `neutral-400`, `neutral-700` | Border of neutral surfaces, tables, dividers, and key caps.                                    |
| `--color-border-hover`         | `neutral-600`, `neutral-500` | Border under the pointer.                                                                      |
| `--color-control-border`       | `neutral-500`                | Resting border of neutral text controls and toggles, drawn at a fraction on text controls.     |
| `--color-background`           | `neutral-50`, `neutral-950`  | The page.                                                                                      |
| `--color-foreground`           | `neutral-100`, `neutral-900` | The quiet background tone one step off the page: neutral soft cards, panels, and alerts.       |
| `--color-surface`              | `neutral-200`, `neutral-800` | A further step: nested and muted surfaces, and the neutral intent's tint.                      |
| `--color-text`                 | `neutral-950`, `neutral-50`  | Body text, and the neutral intent's color.                                                     |
| `--color-text-secondary`       | `neutral-700`, `neutral-400` | Secondary text, such as `.hint`.                                                               |
| `--color-text-contrast`        | `neutral-50`, `neutral-950`  | Text on a full fill of `--color-text`, such as the mark of a checked neutral toggle.           |
| `--color-text-hover`           | `neutral-700`, `neutral-200` | Neutral color under the pointer.                                                               |
| `--color-text-strong`          | `neutral-900`, `neutral-100` | Neutral text, icons, and borders where the fill is not full.                                   |
| `--color-tooltip`              | `white`, `neutral-700`       | Background of a tooltip bubble with no intent. Chosen per theme so it reads as lifted in both. |
| `--color-tooltip-contrast`     | `neutral-900`, `neutral-100` | Text on `--color-tooltip`.                                                                     |
| `--color-success`              | `emerald-700`                | Fill of `.success`.                                                                            |
| `--color-success-contrast`     | `neutral-50`                 | Text on a full success fill: 5.14:1.                                                           |
| `--color-success-hover`        | `#007552`, `#008e66`         | Success fill under the pointer.                                                                |
| `--color-success-subtle`       | `emerald-100`, `emerald-900` | Success tint behind soft components.                                                           |
| `--color-success-strong`       | `emerald-800`, `emerald-300` | Success text, icons, and borders where the fill is not full.                                   |
| `--color-warning`              | `amber-600`                  | Fill of `.warning`.                                                                            |
| `--color-warning-contrast`     | `neutral-950`                | Text on a full warning fill: near-black, not the page color. 6.19:1.                           |
| `--color-warning-hover`        | `#d46700`, `#e78300`         | Warning fill under the pointer.                                                                |
| `--color-warning-subtle`       | `amber-100`, `amber-900`     | Warning tint behind soft components.                                                           |
| `--color-warning-strong`       | `amber-800`, `amber-300`     | Warning text, icons, and borders where the fill is not full.                                   |
| `--color-destructive`          | `rose-700`                   | Fill of `.destructive`.                                                                        |
| `--color-destructive-contrast` | `neutral-50`                 | Text on a full destructive fill: 5.78:1.                                                       |
| `--color-destructive-hover`    | `#c00036`, `#d1054b`         | Destructive fill under the pointer.                                                            |
| `--color-destructive-subtle`   | `rose-100`, `rose-900`       | Destructive tint behind soft components.                                                       |
| `--color-destructive-strong`   | `rose-800`, `rose-300`       | Destructive text, icons, and borders where the fill is not full.                               |
| `--color-info`                 | `indigo-600`                 | Fill of `.info`.                                                                               |
| `--color-info-contrast`        | `neutral-50`                 | Text on a full info fill: 6.19:1.                                                              |
| `--color-info-hover`           | `#4b36e9`, `#5e4ff9`         | Info fill under the pointer.                                                                   |
| `--color-info-subtle`          | `indigo-100`, `indigo-900`   | Info tint behind soft components.                                                              |
| `--color-info-strong`          | `indigo-800`, `indigo-300`   | Info text, icons, and borders where the fill is not full.                                      |

Theme changes belong in these values, not in component rules that check the theme.

## Intent tokens

An intent class sets these seven slots, and components read them. Because every component reads the same seven names, a class that sets all seven works as an intent, as [Your own intent](#your-own-intent) shows.

| Token               | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--intent-color`    | The intent's base color, what a fill is made of.                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `--intent-contrast` | Text on a full fill of `--intent-color`.                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `--intent-hover`    | The base color under the pointer.                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `--intent-strong`   | The intent as text, icon, or border wherever the fill is not full.                                                                                                                                                            |
| `--intent-subtle`   | The light tint behind soft components and progress tracks. Neutral uses `--color-surface`.                                                                                                                                    |
